### WHAT IT IS
The **Computer Training Centres (Regulation) Bill, 2004** is a private member's legislative proposal introduced by Shri Iqbal Ahmed Saradgi, M.P., to regulate private computer training institutions across India [1], [2]. It mandates compulsory registration before running any computer centre, prescribes syllabus and fee caps, provides for complaint handling, and lays down penal sanctions for violations to protect students from unregistered centres and commercial exploitation [1], [3], [4].

### PENAL PROVISIONS UNDER THE BILL
Under **Clause 10** of the Bill, any person who violates the provisions of the Act is liable to the following penal terms [1]:

| Penalty Component | Statutory Prescription |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Minimum Imprisonment** | Term which **shall not be less than three years** [1] |
| **Minimum Fine** | Fine which **shall not be less than one lakh rupees** (₹1,00,000) [1] |

### OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Sponsor / Ownership:** Shri Iqbal Ahmed Saradgi, Member of Parliament (Private Member's Bill) [2].
* **Status:** Introduced legislative proposal (Bill stage, not enacted law) [2].
* **Enforcement Authority:** Appropriate Government (Central Government or State Government, as the case may be) [5].

### DESIGN
* **Mandatory Registration:** Prohibits running any computer centre without prior registration with the appropriate Government (Clause 3) [4].
* **Application Window:** Centre heads must apply within **one month** of commencement (Clause 4) [6].
* **Regulatory Control:** The appropriate Government is mandated to prescribe the syllabus and fees for each course (Clause 7) [3].
* **Grievance Redressal:** Investigations on complaints against centres must be decided within **one month**, leading to cancellation of registration if substantiated (Clauses 8 and 9) [1], [3].

### IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* **Status of the Bill:** The text exists in the parliamentary record as an introduced private member's bill; it was never notified into force [1], [2].
* **Enforcement Discretion:** While the Bill fixes mandatory minimum thresholds for penalties without defining an upper ceiling or alternative compounding mechanisms, its execution remains non-binding without statutory passage [1].

### WHAT IT IS
The **Computer Training Centres (Regulation) Bill, 2004** is a private member's legislative proposal introduced by Shri Iqbal Ahmed Saradgi, M.P., to regulate private computer training institutions across India [1], [2]. It requires compulsory registration of computer centres, empowers governments to set curricula and fees, provides for complaint investigation and cancellation of registration, and establishes penal sanctions to prevent institutions from charging exorbitant fees or shutting down abruptly without completing courses [2], [3], [4].

### OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
- **Proposer / Ownership:** Private Member's Bill introduced by **Shri Iqbal Ahmed Saradgi, M.P.** [1].
- **Appropriate Authority:** Central Government or State Government (as the "appropriate Government") [1], with rule-making powers vested in the Central Government [2].
- **Type & Stage:** As-introduced private member's bill (dated **August 18, 2004**; not enacted law) [2].

### PENALTIES FOR VIOLATION (CLAUSE 10)
Under **Clause 10** of the Bill, any person who violates the provisions of the Act shall be punishable with:
- **Minimum term of imprisonment:** **Not less than three years** [4].
- **Minimum fine:** **Not less than one lakh rupees** (₹1,00,000) [4].

| Violation Aspect | Statutory Stipulation (Clause 10) |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Imprisonment** | Minimum term of **not less than 3 years** [4] |
| **Monetary Fine** | Minimum fine of **not less than ₹1,00,000** [4] |
| **Administrative Action** | Cancellation of centre registration under Clause 9 [4] |

### WHAT IT IS
Under the **Copyright (Second Amendment) Bill, 1992**, the provision proposed to permit adaptation of software for debugging purposes was the insertion of a new **clause (aa)** into sub-section (1) of **section 52** of the Copyright Act, 1957 [3][8]. This was complemented by a related proviso concerning authors' special rights under section 57 [2].

### OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Instrument:** The Copyright (Second Amendment) Bill, 1992 (Bill No. 111 of 1992) [5].
* **Sponsoring Minister:** Arjun Singh, Central Government [11].
* **Nature:** Proposed statutory amendment to the Copyright Act, 1957 [5].
* **Status in Record:** Introduced in Parliament in 1992 [5].

### DESIGN
To accommodate the legitimate needs of lawful users while preventing unauthorized reproduction, the Bill proposed the following mechanisms:

1. **Amendment of Section 52 (Acts not constituting infringement):**
   * **Clause 17** sought to amend section 52(1) by inserting a new **clause (aa)** [3][8]:
     > *"(aa) the making of copies or adaptation of a computer programme by the lawful possessor of a copy of such computer programme, from such copy—*
     > *(i) in order to utilise the computer programme for the purpose for which it was supplied; or*
     > *(ii) to make back-up copies purely as a temporary protection against loss, destruction or damage in order only to utilise the computer programme for the purpose for which it was supplied;"* [8]
   * The *Notes on Clauses* explicitly clarify that this new clause (aa) was inserted to cover the legitimate requirement of the lawful owner/possessor of a copy of a computer programme to make adaptations for **"debugging"** and to make back-up copies [3][7].
   * Concurrently, computer programmes were expressly excluded from general fair dealing for private use under section 52(1)(a) to prevent unwarranted reproduction [3][8].

2. **Proviso on Author's Special Rights:**
   * Consistent with sub-clause (2) of clause 17, a proviso was proposed to be added regarding computer programmes to ensure that adaptation of a computer programme for the purpose commonly known as **"debugging"** was made permissible without violating the author's special moral rights [2].

### TRADE-OFFS
* **Case for:** Legitimate software owners require operational flexibility to correct errors (debug) and ensure functionality to utilize software for its supplied purpose without risking civil infringement or criminal penalties [3][8].
* **Case against / Regulatory Guardrail:** A blanket reproduction right under "private use" was seen as vulnerable to piracy; thus, the exception was narrowly confined to lawful possessors strictly for the purpose for which the software was supplied or for temporary back-up protection [3][8].

### IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* **Statutory evolution:** Track the subsequent formulation of these debugging and interoperability provisions as eventually enacted in the Copyright (Amendment) Act, 1994, and further refined via clauses (ab), (ac), and (ad) introduced under the Copyright (Amendment) Bill, 1999 [14].

### WHAT IT IS
Under the **Copyright (Second Amendment) Bill, 1992**, the adaptation of software for debugging purposes was provided for by inserting an exemption into **Section 52(1)** of the Copyright Act, 1957 [3][8]. This was aimed at accommodating the legitimate requirements of lawful users to adapt software and create backup copies without infringing copyright [3].

### STATUTORY PROVISIONS PROPOSED
1. **Insertion of Section 52(1)(aa)**: 
   Clause 17(3) of the Bill proposed to insert clause `(aa)` into Section 52(1), explicitly stating that the following acts shall not constitute an infringement of copyright [8]:
   > *"the making of copies or adaptation of a computer programme by the lawful possessor of a copy of such computer programme, from such copy—*
   > *(i) in order to utilise the computer programme for the purpose for which it was supplied; or*
   > *(ii) to make back-up copies purely as a temporary protection against loss, destruction or damage in order only to utilise the computer programme for the purpose for which it was supplied;"* [8]
   
   As explained in the Bill's *Notes on Clauses*, this provision was introduced specifically *"to cover the legitimate requirement of the lawful owner of a copy of a computer programme to make adaptations for 'debugging' and to make back-up copies"* [3][7].

2. **Exclusion from General Fair Use under Section 52(1)(a)**:
   The Bill simultaneously amended Section 52(1)(a) to insert *", not being computer programme,"* after *"artistic work"*, removing computer programs from general private reproduction/study exceptions because a general right to reproduce them for private use was deemed unnecessary and susceptible to abuse [3][8].

3. **Proviso to Section 57 (Author's Special Rights)**:
   Consistent with the adaptation exception in Section 52(1)(aa), Clause 20 of the Bill amended Section 57(1) by adding a proviso to ensure that the author's moral rights could not be invoked against lawful adaptation [2][17]:
   > *"Provided that the author shall not have any right to restrain or claim damages in respect of any adaptation of a computer programme to which clause (aa) of sub-section (1) of section 52 applies."* [2][17]

### WHAT IT IS
The **Special Educational Facilities for Children of Manual Scavengers Bill, 2001** is a private member's legislative proposal introduced in the Rajya Sabha by Shri S. S. Ahluwalia to provide free and comprehensive educational entitlements to children born of scavengers or safai karamcharis [1, 9].

### OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Authority:** The "appropriate Government" is defined under Clause 2(a) as the **State Government** in the case of a State, and the **Central Government** in other cases [1].
* **Status:** Introduced in the **Rajya Sabha** as Bill No. LXX of 2001 [1].
* **Statutory Nature:** Private Member's Bill (as introduced, not enacted) [1, 9].

### MANDATED SURVEY RESPONSIBILITY (CLAUSE 3)
Under **Clause 3** of the Bill, specific statutory obligations are assigned to the appropriate government regarding the identification of eligible children [3]:
1. **Conduct of Survey:** It is the duty of the appropriate government to conduct a survey within the area under its jurisdiction to identify the children of scavengers [3].
2. **Preparation of Beneficiary List:** The appropriate government must prepare a list, in such manner as may be prescribed by rules, of those children who are to be imparted education by that government [3].
3. **Periodic Revision:** The appropriate government is required to cause the list of eligible children to be revised at such intervals as may be prescribed [3].

### ASSOCIATED ADMINISTRATIVE & FINANCIAL PROVISIONS
* **Definition of Target Group:** A "scavenger" is defined under Clause 2(e) as a person who had been engaged or employed for manually carrying human excreta prior to the commencement of the Employment of Manual Scavengers and Construction of Dry Latrines (Prohibition) Act, 1993 [10].
* **Enforcement Machinery:** Under Clause 7, the appropriate government may appoint **Attendance Authorities** and assisting personnel to oversee attendance and implementation [5].
* **Projected Financial Requirement:** The Bill's Financial Memorandum estimated a recurring expenditure of approximately **₹100 crore per annum** from the Consolidated Fund of India, alongside an estimated non-recurring outlay of **₹10 crore** [2].

### WHAT IT IS
The **Special Educational Facilities for Children of Manual Scavengers Bill, 2001** is a private member's legislative proposal introduced in the Rajya Sabha by Shri S. S. Ahluwalia to provide free and comprehensive educational support—spanning school level to post-graduate, technical, and medical education—to children of scavengers or Safai Karamcharis who were historically engaged in manual scavenging [1][4][9].

### OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Sponsor / Instrument:** Private Member's Bill introduced in the Rajya Sabha (Bill No. LXX of 2001) [1][9].
* **Appropriate Government:** Defined under **Clause 2(a)** as the **State Government** in the case of a State, and the **Central Government** in other cases [1].
* **Status:** As-introduced text (not enacted into law) [1].

### IDENTIFICATION RESPONSIBILITIES (DESIGN)
Under **Clause 3** of the Bill, the responsibility for identifying eligible beneficiaries is placed squarely on the appropriate government through mandatory surveys and record-keeping [3]:

| Obligation | Statutory Provision | Mandated Action |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Jurisdictional Survey** | Clause 3 | Duty to conduct a survey in the area under its jurisdiction to identify the children of scavengers who are to be imparted education [2][3]. |
| **Beneficiary List** | Clause 3 | Duty to prepare a list of such eligible children in such manner as may be prescribed [3]. |
| **Periodic Revision** | Clause 3 | Duty to cause the list to be revised at such intervals as may be prescribed [3]. |

For identification purposes, **Clause 2(e)** defines a "Scavenger" as a person who had been engaged or employed for manually carrying human excreta before the commencement of the *Employment of Manual Scavengers and Construction of Dry Latrines (Prohibition) Act, 1993* [10].

### TRADE-OFFS
* **Case For:** Directly attacks the generational perpetuation of manual scavenging by creating state-funded pathways to primary, technical, and professional education, accompanied by stipends, books, uniforms, and boarding [4][11].
* **Case Against:** Imposes an open-ended financial commitment (estimated in the Financial Memorandum at ₹100 crore recurring annually and ₹10 crore non-recurring) and heavy administrative burdens of continuous surveying and tracking via Attendance Authorities across State jurisdictions without specified inter-tier cost sharing [2][5].

### IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* **Rule-Making Powers:** The manner of conducting surveys and the intervals for list revisions rely entirely on delegated rules to be framed by the Central Government under **Clause 9** [6].
* **Enforcement Machinery:** Deployment and staffing of Attendance Authorities under **Clause 7** to monitor attendance and determine whether economic circumstances warrant part-time institution attendance under **Clause 8** [5][6].

### WHAT IT IS
The **Right to Work Bill, 2002** is a Private Member's Bill introduced in the Lok Sabha by Shri G. M. Banatwalla to provide every eligible citizen with a statutory right to work or an unemployment allowance (not less than ₹200 per week) until appropriate work is provided [1, 2]. To finance this allowance and related administrative expenditure, the Bill provides for the establishment of a dedicated **Right to Work Fund** [1, 3].

### OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Chamber & Sponsor:** Introduced in Lok Sabha as a Private Member's Bill by Shri G. M. Banatwalla, M.P. [1, 4].
* **Relevant Ministry:** Ministry of Labour (Presidential recommendation conveyed under Articles 117 and 274 of the Constitution via Ministry of Labour letter dated 19 April 2002) [4].
* **Status:** Proposed statutory measure (Bill as introduced) [1].

### MANDATED REVENUE SOURCES CREDITED TO THE FUND
Under **Section 9(3)** of the Right to Work Bill, 2002, the following five sources of revenue are mandated to be credited to the Right to Work Fund [3]:

| Clause | Revenue Source |
|---|---|
| **Section 9(3)(a)** | All grants made by the Central Government under Section 9(2) [3] |
| **Section 9(3)(b)** | All voluntary donations made to the Fund (which qualify for income-tax rebate/deduction under Section 11) [3, 5] |
| **Section 9(3)(c)** | All contributions in respect of the Right to Work Insurance Policy under Section 10 [3] |
| **Section 9(3)(d)** | All sums collected under Section 12 (contributions at a prescribed rate from citizens who secure work after registration) [3, 5, 6] |
| **Section 9(3)(e)** | Any interest, dividend, or other return on any investment made out of any part of the Fund [3] |

### DESIGN & ALLOCATION RULES
* **Outflow:** All amounts due and payable under the Act and all expenditure relating to the management and administration of the Fund are required to be paid out of the Fund under **Section 9(4)** [3].
* **Reporting:** The Central Government is required under **Section 14** to prepare a general annual report on the working and administration of the Fund and implementation of the Act after each financial year to be laid before each House of Parliament [7].

### IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* **Rule-Making Tracking:** Specific rates and rules governing contributions under Section 12 and insurance details under Section 10 are delegated to Central Government notification under Section 15(2) [6].
* **Legislative Progress:** **Not in record.**

### **WHAT IT IS**
The Right to Work Bill, 2002 is a Private Member's Bill introduced in the Lok Sabha by Shri G. M. Banatwalla, M.P. [1, 2]. It seeks to confer a statutory right to work on eligible adult citizens registered at employment exchanges, provides for a weekly allowance (not less than ₹200 per week) until appropriate work is provided, and establishes a dedicated "Right to Work Fund" to finance these allowances [1, 3, 4].

### **OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS**
* **Sponsor / Ministry:** Introduced by Shri G. M. Banatwalla, M.P.; recommendation for introduction and consideration conveyed by the Minister of Labour under Articles 117(1), 117(3), and 274(1) of the Constitution [1, 5].
* **Legal Status:** Bill as introduced (not enacted into law) [1].
* **Statutory Body / Fund Owner:** Central Government [3, 4].

### **MANDATED REVENUE SOURCES OF THE FUND**
Under **Section 9(3)** of the Bill, the following five sources of revenue are mandated to be credited to the Right to Work Fund [6, 7]:

| Provision | Mandated Revenue Source |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Section 9(3)(a)** | All grants made by the Central Government under Section 9(2) [6, 7]. |
| **Section 9(3)(b)** | All voluntary donations made to the Fund (which qualify for income-tax rebate/deduction under Section 11) [6, 7, 8]. |
| **Section 9(3)(c)** | All contributions in respect of the Right to Work Insurance Policy under Section 10 [6, 7]. |
| **Section 9(3)(d)** | All sums collected under Section 12 (mandatory contributions at a prescribed rate and period from every citizen who receives work or allowance under the Act after securing employment) [6, 7, 9]. |
| **Section 9(3)(e)** | Any interest, dividend, or other return on any investment made out of any part of the Fund [7]. |

### **TRADE-OFFS**
* **Case For:** Creates a legally enforceable safety net guaranteeing ₹200 per week minimum sustenance or public employment, building a diversified multi-source fund that reduces government fiscal burden over time through beneficiary contributions and private donations [4, 8, 10].
* **Case Against:** Projected recurring liability on the Consolidated Fund of India of approximately ₹500 crore per annum, along with the administrative complexity of tracking post-employment clawback contributions from beneficiaries under Section 12 [9, 10].

### **IMPLEMENTATION WATCH**
* **Rule-Making Power (Section 15):** Notification of rules specifying the contribution rate and duration under Section 12, tax deduction criteria under Section 11, and insurance policy modalities under Section 10 [9, 11].
* **Parliamentary Accountability (Section 14):** Laying of the general annual report on the working and administration of the Fund before both Houses of Parliament [12].

### **WHAT IT IS**
Under the **Merchant Shipping (Amendment) Bill, 2004** (enacted as the **Merchant Shipping (Amendment) Act, 2007**), a **recognised security organisation** is defined under the newly inserted **Section 344K(f)** of Part IXB of the *Merchant Shipping Act, 1958* [1][2]. To qualify for designation and authorisation by the Central Government, an entity must satisfy specific substantive competence and legal formalisation criteria [1][2].

### **OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS**
* **Statutory Provision:** Section 344K(f) read with the proviso to Section 344M(2) of the *Merchant Shipping Act, 1958* [1][2][3].
* **Designating Authority:** Central Government (via notification in the Official Gazette) [1][2].
* **Legislative Stage:** Introduced in the Lok Sabha on **23 December 2004**; passed by the Lok Sabha on **14 August 2007**; passed by the Rajya Sabha on **6 September 2007**; and received presidential assent on **24 September 2007** (Act No. 40 of 2007) [4].

### **DESIGN & QUALIFYING CRITERIA**
According to Section 344K(f), an entity qualifies as a recognised security organisation if it meets the following conditions [1][2]:

1. **Organizational Form:** It must be an *"organisation, company, firm or body of individuals"* [1][2].
2. **Subject-Matter Competence:** It must possess:
   * Expertise in matters relating to **security** [1][2]; and
   * Knowledge of **ship and port operations** [1][2].
3. **Government Authorisation:** It must be authorised by the Central Government by notification in the **Official Gazette** [1][2].
4. **Statutory Mandate:** The authorisation empowers the entity to carry out:
   * Assessment, verification, approval, or certification required under **Part IXB** or by the **International Ship and Port Facility Security Code (ISPS Code)** [1][2]; and
   * Any security measures under **Section 344M** on behalf of the Central Government, subject to prescribed conditions [3].

### **TRADE-OFFS**
* **Strongest Case For:** Enables the Central Government to leverage specialized technical bodies to conduct assessments, verifications, and security audits required under the ISPS Code and the Safety Convention (SOLAS 1974), ensuring Indian ships and ports satisfy international clearance standards [2][5].
* **Strongest Case Against:** Outsources sensitive port and vessel security evaluations to external entities, requiring strict oversight to prevent security lapses, conflicts of interest, or inadequate compliance rigor [1][3].

### **IMPLEMENTATION WATCH**
* **Official Gazette Notifications:** Track gazette notifications issued by the Ministry designating authorized recognized security organisations under Section 344K(f) [1][2].
* **Rules and Conditions:** Monitor delegated rules framed under Section 344M and Section 344T regulating fees, certifications, and operational boundaries of recognized security organisations [3][6].

### WHAT IT IS
Under the **Merchant Shipping (Amendment) Bill, 2004**, a **recognised security organisation** is defined under proposed **Section 344K(f)** as any organisation, company, firm, or body of individuals having expertise in matters relating to security and knowledge of ship and port operations [1], [2].

### OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Designating Authority:** The **Central Government** [1], [2].
* **Instrument of Authorization:** Official notification in the **Official Gazette** [2].
* **Statutory Location:** Part IX B (incorporating maritime security provisions in line with the International Ship and Port Facility Security Code / Safety Convention) [2], [3].

### DESIGN & QUALIFYING CRITERIA
To qualify and be designated by the Central Government, an entity must satisfy the statutory definition set out in Section 344K(f) [1], [2]:

| Requirement Type | Statutory Condition |
|---|---|
| **Form of Entity** | Any organisation, company, firm, or body of individuals [1]. |
| **Subject Expertise** | Proven expertise in matters relating to security [1]. |
| **Operational Knowledge** | Knowledge of ship and port operations [1]. |
| **Statutory Mandate / Purpose** | Authorized to carry out assessment, verification, approval, or certification required by Part IX B or by the International Ship and Port Facility Security (ISPS) Code [2]. |

Any further detailed procedural eligibility criteria, rules, or benchmarks beyond these express statutory terms are **Not in record.**

### TRADE-OFFS
* **Case For:** Enables the deployment of specialized technical bodies to conduct security assessments, plan verifications, and compliance certifications under the ISPS Code, ensuring Indian vessels and port facilities maintain international maritime security standards and secure unimpeded entry into foreign ports [2], [3], [4].
* **Case Against:** **Not in record.**

### IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* Track notifications issued in the Official Gazette specifying authorized security organisations under Section 344K(f) and rules formulated under Section 344T for maritime security verification and certification [2], [5].

### WHAT IT IS
Under the **National Rural Employment Guarantee Bill, 2004**, the statutory standard workday duration specified for setting the schedule of rates of wages for unskilled manual labour is **seven hours** [1]. 

### OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Sponsoring Authority:** Introduced by the Central Government; implemented through State Governments, Programme Officers, and Gram Panchayats [2], [3].
* **Instrument Type:** Statutory legislation (**National Rural Employment Guarantee Bill, 2004** / enacted as Act No. 42 of 2005) [1], [4].
* **Statutory Baseline:** Clause 8 of **Schedule I** (*Minimum Features of a Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme*, under Section 4(3)) mandates that the schedule of rates of wages for unskilled labourers must be fixed so that an individual working for **seven hours** normally earns a wage equal to the statutory wage rate [1].

### DESIGN & WAGE PARAMETERS
* **Workday Standard:** Exactly **7 hours** of work serves as the standard labour quantum baseline for fixing output norms/piece rates [1].
* **Wage Rate Floor:** The Bill provides that the wage rate specified by the Central Government shall not be less than **₹60 per day** [5].
* **Parity Requirement:** When piece-rate wage schedules are configured by the state, task measurements must ensure that standard output over a 7-hour workday equates to the notified daily wage rate [1].

### TRADE-OFFS
* **Labour Protection (Pro):** Establishing a rigid 7-hour productivity baseline prevents unrealistic workload norms that would otherwise dilute statutory daily minimum wages for manual labourers [1].
* **Administrative Rigidity (Con):** Setting uniform piece-rate outputs calibrated to a standard 7-hour threshold across diverse topographies, soil conditions, and seasonal climates creates difficulties for local implementing agencies without extensive work-study revisions [1].

### IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* **Schedule of Rates (SoR) Calibration:** Tracking state-level Rural Development Department notifications to ensure task rates for earthwork and excavation reflect a genuine 7-hour output ceiling [1].
* **Muster Roll & Measurement Verification:** Scrutiny of field measurements taken by Programme Officers and Gram Panchayats to prevent contractor deductions or understated piece earnings [1], [3].

### WHAT IT IS
The National Rural Employment Guarantee framework provides a statutory guarantee of at least **100 days** of wage employment in a financial year to every rural household whose adult members volunteer to do unskilled manual work [1][2]. Where wages are directly linked to the quantity of work performed (piece-rate basis), the schedule of rates fixed by the State Government must benchmark output against a standard workday so that labourers normally earn the statutory daily wage rate [3].

### OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Ministry / Government Level:** Central Government specifies base wage rates, while the **State Government** formulates and notifies the Scheme and fixes the piece-rate schedule of rates in consultation with the State Employment Guarantee Council [3][4].
* **Instrument:** Statutory legislation introduced as **The National Rural Employment Guarantee Bill, 2004** (enacted as Act No. 42 of 2005) [2][5].

### DESIGN: STANDARD WORKDAY DURATION
Under the provisions governing minimum features of rural employment guarantee schemes:
* **Workday Duration:** The schedule of rates of wages for unskilled labourers must be fixed such that a person working for **seven hours** would normally earn a wage equal to the prescribed daily wage rate [3].
* **Rate-Setting Rule:** When wages are linked to the quantity of work, payment follows a schedule of rates fixed every year by the State Government in consultation with the State Council [3].
* **Wage Floor Protection:** Under no circumstances shall workers be paid less than the statutory wage rate [3], which cannot be fixed at less than **₹60 per day** under the Act [4].

### TRADE-OFFS
* **Strongest Case For:** Protects piece-rate workers from unreasonable workload norms by tying piece rates directly to a standard **7-hour** physical labour threshold, preventing underpayment and excessive physical strain [3].
* **Strongest Case Against:** Productivity and terrain vary significantly across regions; rigid standard-day assumptions can lead to administrative disputes in measuring daily piece-work outputs across different geographic conditions.

### IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* **Annual Revision of Rates:** Annual notification by State Governments of the schedule of rates in consultation with State Councils [3].
* **Measurement & Disbursal:** Adherence to weekly or fortnightly disbursement timelines without falling below the daily wage rate floor [3][6].

### WHAT IT IS
Under the **Institutes of Technology (Amendment) Bill, 2001**, the University of Roorkee was converted into an Indian Institute of Technology (**IIT Roorkee**) and declared an institution of national importance [1], [2]. To ensure institutional continuity during the transition, Section 6 of the Bill inserted transitional provisions into Section 38 of the Institutes of Technology Act, 1961, governing preexisting administrative and academic authorities [3], [4].

### OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Ministry:** Department of Secondary and Higher Education, Ministry of Human Resource Development [5].
* **Instrument:** Statutory Bill to replace the Institutes of Technology (Amendment) Ordinance, 2001 (promulgated on **21 September 2001**) and repeal the Roorkee University Act, 1947 [1], [6].
* **Status / Commencement:** Deemed to have come into force on **21 September 2001** [7].

### DESIGN & INTERIM ARRANGEMENTS FOR THE ACADEMIC COUNCIL
Under **Section 6** of the Bill (inserting clause `(f)` into Section 38 of the principal Act), the specific interim arrangements governing the Academic Council are [3], [4]:

* **Continuance of Functioning:** The Academic Council of the University of Roorkee functioning immediately before the commencement of the Act continues to function as such for IIT Roorkee until a new Senate is constituted under the Act [4].
* **Cessation of Office:** On the formal constitution of the new Senate of IIT Roorkee under the Act, all members of the erstwhile Academic Council holding office immediately before such constitution vacate and cease to hold office [4].
* **Statutes and Ordinances Baseline:** Under clause `(g)` of the inserted provisions, until the first Statutes and Ordinances for IIT Roorkee are framed, the Statutes and Ordinances of **IIT Bombay** (as in force immediately prior to the commencement of the Act) apply to IIT Roorkee with necessary adaptations and modifications, so long as they are not inconsistent with the Act [8].

### TRADE-OFFS
* **Institutional Continuity:** Prevents an administrative and academic vacuum, ensuring ongoing degree programmes, examinations, and university operations run without disruption while statutory bodies are constituted [1], [4].
* **Temporary Governance Friction:** Existing state-university academic governance structures temporarily exercise IIT Senate-level functions under transplanted IIT Bombay statutes, pending fresh body nominations [4], [8].

### IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* Formal constitution and notification of the IIT Roorkee Senate to effectuate the complete dissolution of the transitional Academic Council [4].
* Promulgation and notification of IIT Roorkee's first Statutes and Ordinances to replace the interim application of IIT Bombay regulations [8].

### WHAT IT IS
Under the **Institutes of Technology (Amendment) Bill, 2001**, the interim transitional arrangements mandate that the Academic Council of the University of Roorkee continues its functions for the newly incorporated Indian Institute of Technology, Roorkee until a formal Senate is constituted [1][2].

### OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Ministry / Department**: Department of Secondary and Higher Education, Ministry of Human Resource Development [5].
* **Instrument Type**: Statutory amendment to the Institutes of Technology Act, 1961 (replacing the Institutes of Technology (Amendment) Ordinance, 2001) [3][4].
* **Specific Provision**: Clause 6 of the Bill, inserting clause (f) into Section 38 (transitional provisions) of the principal Act [1][2].

### DESIGN & INTERIM ARRANGEMENTS
| Institution Body | Interim Authority / Arrangement | Cessation Condition |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Academic Council** | Continues functioning as such for IIT Roorkee as it functioned immediately prior to commencement [1][2]. | Members cease to hold office automatically upon the constitution of a new Senate under the Act [1][2]. |
| **Statutes & Ordinances** | Until the first Statutes and Ordinances of IIT Roorkee are framed, the Statutes and Ordinances of IIT Bombay apply with necessary modifications and adaptations [1]. | Cease when IIT Roorkee's own first Statutes and Ordinances are made under the Act [1]. |

### TRADE-OFFS
* **Administrative Continuity (Case For)**: Prevents an academic governance void during the conversion of the University of Roorkee into an IIT, allowing academic regulation and curricula to function uninterrupted while shifting admissions to the Joint Entrance Examination (JEE) framework [2][4].

For subscribers in the **Mumbai** service area wishing to obtain a Unique Porting Code (UPC), Unitech Wireless requested TRAI to facilitate a special porting mechanism permitting it to accept requests for UPC generation through three specific channels [1]:

2. **Company owned company operated (COCO) stores** [1]
3. **Authorised direct franchisees** [1]

Unitech Wireless proposed that following due verification of subscriber details across these touchpoints, the UPC would be generated manually for the requested mobile number to enable porting to other operators [1].

*(Note: In its subsequent direction issued on 22 February 2013, TRAI directed Unitech Wireless specifically to accept UPC generation requests at its call centres after verification of subscriber details and publish the call centre contact details and procedures in newspapers and on its website [2, 3]).*

### **WHAT IT IS**
Following the Supreme Court direction of 15 February 2013 leading to the discontinuance of its operations, **M/s Unitech Wireless (Tamilnadu) Private Limited** submitted a proposal to the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) to facilitate porting out for its subscribers via an alternative mechanism, as consumers could not generate a Unique Porting Code (UPC) via standard SMS channels due to service shutdowns [1, 2].

### **PROPOSED SPECIAL CHANNELS**
In its letter dated **19 February 2013**, Unitech Wireless proposed to accept requests for UPC generation from Mumbai service area subscribers through three dedicated channels [1]:

1. **Call centres** [1]
2. **Company-owned company-operated (COCO) stores** [1]
3. **Authorised direct franchisees** [1]

Under this proposal, after verifying subscriber details, the UPC would be generated manually for the requested mobile number to enable porting to other telecom operators [1].

### **REGULATORY OUTCOME**
In its subsequent direction dated **22 February 2013**, TRAI directed Unitech Wireless to accept requests for generation of UPC specifically at its **call centres** after subscriber verification, and to widely publish the contact details of the call centres along with the porting and refund procedure on its website and in newspapers [2, 3].

### WHAT IT IS
In regulatory proceedings concerning Lifecell International Pvt. Ltd. (LIPL), an umbilical cord blood stem cell banking provider, the Director General (Investigation & Registration) of the erstwhile Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices Commission (MRTPC) alleged violations concerning marketing claims and contractual liability terms [1, 2].

### PROVISIONS ALLEGEDLY VIOLATED

| Allegation | Nature of Practice | MRTP Act Provision Invoked |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Unsubstantiated marketing claims** (claiming "Lifecell" is "No.1 Stem Cell Technology" and the "first and only accredited Cord Blood Stem Cell Bank in India") | Unfair Trade Practice (UTP) | **Section 36A(1)(i), (ii), (iv), and (vi)** [2] |
| **Limited liability clauses in customer agreements** (incorporating Clause 12 limiting liability in case of loss of specimen, allegedly imposing unjustified costs via service conditions) | Restrictive Trade Practice (RTP) / Unfair Trade Practice | **Section 2(o)** [2] *(also initially noted under **Section 36A** by the MRTP Commission)* [1] |

### REGULATORY FINDING
Following the transfer of the case to the Competition Commission of India (CCI) under Section 66 of the Competition Act, 2002, the CCI determined that [1, 2, 3]:
- LIPL provided facts and figures demonstrating that it had tested 16,000 samples, possessed storage capacity for over 100,000 samples, and maintained technical collaboration with Cryo-Cell International; there was no evidence demonstrating that the marketing representation was false [3, 4].
- LIPL amended the impugned limited liability clause (replacing Clause 12 with Clause 11) effective 8 April 2009, and comparable contractual limited liability terms were standard industry practice across stem cell banking companies, meaning no restrictive trade practice was established [3, 5].

### 1. WHAT IT IS
**Scholarships for Higher Education for Young Achievers (SHREYAS) for Scheduled Castes (SCs)** is a Central Sector Umbrella Scheme administered by the Central Government to provide financial assistance and scholarships to students belonging to the Scheduled Caste (SC) category [1][2]. The umbrella framework comprises four sub-schemes: the **Top Class Scholarship Scheme for SC students (TCS)**, the **Free Coaching Scheme for SC and OBC students (FCS)**, the **National Overseas Scholarship Scheme for Scheduled Castes etc. (NOS)**, and the **National Fellowship for Scheduled Caste students (NFSC)** [1].

### 2. OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Ministry / Department**: Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment (Department of Social Justice and Empowerment) [1][2].
* **Instrument Type**: Central Sector Scheme [1][3].
* **Status**: In active implementation across the country [1][3].

### 3. FUNDING RELEASED TO BIHAR (FY 2021-22 TO FY 2023-24)
According to Ministry data furnished in parliamentary records:
* Total funds released under **SHREYAS** during the three-year period from **2021-22 to 2023-24** for the State of **Bihar** amounted to **₹21.36 crore** [2].
* *Annual breakdown*: The specific year-by-year disbursement breakdown strictly for Bihar across each of the three individual financial years is **Not in record.** (parliamentary replies note that because SHREYAS is a Central Sector Umbrella Scheme, funds are not routinely maintained on an earmarked State-wise/district-wise allocation basis) [3].

### 4. TRADE-OFFS
* **Support for Centralised Administration**: Central sector implementation enables Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) and direct fellowship/scholarship awards to eligible students without administrative friction or procedural delays at the State treasury level [1][3].
* **State-Level Visibility Gaps**: Because funds flow centrally through national portals and schemes to individual scholars and institutions, disaggregated district-wise and annual state-level tracking remains limited in the institutional record [2][3].

### 5. IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* **Scheme Outreach**: Track regional awareness campaigns, including regional newspaper insertions and State Principal Secretary coordination, to improve uptake in targeted regions [4].
* **Component Tracking**: Monitor individual allocations across TCS, FCS, NOS, and NFSC via central portals [1][3].

### WHAT IT IS
Garima Grehs are shelter homes established under the SMILE scheme (**Support for Marginalized Individuals for Livelihood and Enterprise**) to provide safe residential shelter, basic necessities, capacity-building, and social protection to transgender persons to prevent atrocities and enable mainstreaming into respectable livelihoods [1], [2], [3].

### OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Ministry / Department**: Department of Social Justice and Empowerment (DoSJE), Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment [1], [2].
* **Instrument & Scheme Component**: Implemented under the central sector sub-scheme entitled *“Central Sector Scheme for Comprehensive Rehabilitation for Welfare of Transgender Persons”* under the umbrella SMILE scheme [2], [4].
* **Status**: Executive scheme; operational. As of August 2025, **18 Garima Grehs** are supported across 15 States/UTs housing **429 residents**, with approvals sanctioned for **3 new Garima Grehs** (in Jharkhand, Manipur, and Madhya Pradesh) for FY 2025–26 [1], [5].

### DESIGN

| Dimension | Description / Provisions in Record |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Core Facilities** | Safe residential stay, food, medical care, yoga, meditation, and recreational amenities [1]. |
| **Support Services** | In-house mental health counselling via an assigned Counsellor at each home [3]; linkage to MoHFW's 24x7 **Tele MANAS** helpline (14416) for continuous psychosocial support [3]; capacity-building, life-skills training, and skill development to facilitate respectable livelihood mainstreaming [1]; protection of rights and safeguards against atrocities [1]. |
| **Total Funding** | **₹8.25 crore** has been released and utilised by the Garima Grehs under the SMILE scheme [3]. |

### TRADE-OFFS
* **Strengths on Record**: Provides integrated institutional care combining basic shelter with mental health counselling, legal safeguard protections, and vocational/life skill readiness to prevent destitution [1], [3]. Across the wider sub-scheme, **1,404 persons** have been rehabilitated and **725 persons** received skill development training (initiated in FY 2024–25) [2], [4].
* **Gaps on Record**: Geographic spread remains constrained. Recommendations are pending from **14 States/UTs** on proposals forwarded from NGOs/CSOs, while **8 States/UTs** have submitted no proposals for setting up Garima Grehs at all [5].

### IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* **State Approval Pipeline**: Tracking the conversion of pending proposals across the 14 States/UTs and rollout in the 8 States/UTs with zero proposals [5].
* **New Sanctions**: Operationalisation of the 3 newly approved homes sanctioned in FY 2025–26 across Jharkhand, Manipur, and Madhya Pradesh [1].
* **District Awareness**: Monitoring district-level awareness campaigns carried out by State/UT administrations to boost community uptake [3].

### WHAT IT IS
**Garima Greh** (Shelter Home for Transgender Persons) is an initiative under the Support for Marginalized Individuals for Livelihood and Enterprise (**SMILE**) scheme, specifically under its sub-scheme *Central Sector Scheme for Comprehensive Rehabilitation for Welfare of Transgender Persons* [4]. It provides safe residential shelter to transgender persons along with basic amenities, medical assistance, mental health counselling, and skill-building interventions designed to safeguard rights, prevent atrocities, and mainstream residents into respectable livelihoods upon departure [1, 3].

---

### OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Nodal Ministry / Department:** Department of Social Justice and Empowerment (DoSJE), Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment [1, 2, 8].
* **Scheme Classification:** Central Sector Scheme (sub-scheme under SMILE) [4].
* **Operational Footprint:** As per parliamentary replies up to **19 August 2025**, **18 Garima Grehs** are supported across **15 States/UTs**, housing **429 residents** [3, 9]. Three additional homes were sanctioned for **FY 2025–26** in Jharkhand, Manipur, and Madhya Pradesh [2, 9].

---

### DESIGN: FACILITIES, SERVICES & FUNDING

| Pillar | Details from the Official Record |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Core Residential Amenities** | Safe residential shelter equipped with food, medical care, yoga, meditation, and recreational facilities [3]. |
| **Mental Health Support** | Dedicated in-house Counsellor at each Garima Greh [1]; linkage with **Tele MANAS** (24x7 toll-free helpline `14416` by MoHFW) for round-the-clock psychosocial support and counselling [1]. |
| **Skill Development & Livelihood** | Capacity-building and life-skills training to facilitate transition out of shelter homes into sustainable, respectable employment [3]. |
| **Protection & Rights** | Institutional mechanisms to safeguard transgender persons' rights and shield them from atrocities [1, 3]. |
| **Funding Released & Utilised** | **₹8.25 crore** released and utilised by Garima Grehs under the SMILE scheme to date [1, 3]. |

---

### TRADE-OFFS
* **Strongest Case For:** Provides an integrated, secure residential safety net combining basic shelter, structured psychosocial care, and livelihood retraining to prevent destitution and violence against transgender persons [1, 3].
* **Strongest Case Against:** Geographic unevenness and slow expansion; proposals forwarded to **14 States/UTs** remain pending for recommendation, while **8 States/UTs** have submitted no proposals for establishing Garima Grehs [9].

---

### IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* **Proposal Clearance:** State-level clearances for pending proposals forwarded to 14 States/UTs [9].
* **Expansion Pipeline:** Operationalisation of the 3 newly sanctioned homes in Jharkhand, Manipur, and Madhya Pradesh during FY 2025–26 [2, 9].
* **Coverage Gaps:** Engagement with the 8 States/UTs that have yet to submit any project proposals [9].
